passage: As societies transition toward renewable energy sources such as solar and wind power, electrical grids face a fundamental engineering challenge: intermittency. Unlike coal or natural gas plants that can generate electricity continuously on demand, solar panels stop producing after sunset and wind turbines sit idle during calm weather. To prevent blackouts when weather conditions shift abruptly, utility operators require large-scale energy storage systems capable of capturing surplus electricity during peak generation and releasing it when demand surges. While lithium-ion batteries currently dominate short-term grid stabilization, emerging alternatives—including pumped hydroelectric reservoirs, green hydrogen, and iron-air batteries—promise cost-effective storage across days or entire seasons. Developing a diverse portfolio of storage technologies is therefore indispensable for transforming variable renewable energy into a reliable, round-the-clock power supply.
